messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Ricardo Vega was sixty-two years old, a psychiatrist who had built a quiet life in a Midwestern city after fleeing his home country twenty-three years ago. In his early forties, he had been a young faculty member at a university hospital in a capital city that saw a military crackdown on dissidents. Because he treated patients from the opposition movement, he was detained by armed men in uniform, taken to a basement, and interrogated for three days. What he remembered most vividly—and he still remembered it with a clarity that seemed impossible—was the confusion of languages: his captors spoke Spanish but used coded military jargon and shouted fragmented orders, so that the words swirled around him, indistinguishable from the blow of a rifle butt against his ribs or the crackle of a radio. Some moments of those seventy-two hours were excruciatingly clear—the weight of a boot on his hand, the smell of diesel and sweat—while entire hours were blank, as though erased. No one was ever held accountable. The institution he had served and trusted had not only failed to protect him but had participated in his torture. He left his country and every connection he had, and he had never really found a new community.

In the United States, Ricardo worked as a staff psychiatrist in a community mental health center. The job required him to see patients, attend meetings, and talk to colleagues—and he had become expert at rehearsing what he would say before every interaction, running through possible questions and his answers while he walked down the hall. It helped him feel prepared, but the problem was that the preparation itself often triggered the memory: once he started mentally scripting a conversation, fragments of the interrogation would surface—the way an officer had repeated his own name back to him in a mocking tone, the feel of the tape around his wrists. He would then actively redirect his thoughts, forcing himself to think of something else, a technique he had mastered. It worked briefly, but the memories returned without warning at other times—a security guard’s badge glinting under fluorescent lights could instantly bring back the full sensory reliving, his heart hammering, the smell of the basement flooding his nose. When he saw a uniformed police officer in the clinic parking lot, it did not just trigger the memory; it also rekindled his bitter appraisal that the institutions meant to serve the public had betrayed him, and that the people responsible for his suffering walked free. That appraisal, in turn, made uniformed figures feel even more menacing, so that his heart raced before he had consciously registered the sight. And the memory itself—the clarity of certain blows, the blank gaps where he could remember only the sound of incomprehensible chatter—reinforced his sense that his community was gone forever, because the people who had surrounded him then were either dead or scattered, and no one in his present life knew what had happened to him.

Ricardo had come to believe that it was unsafe to go out unless absolutely necessary. He avoided public spaces: the grocery store, the movie theater, even the hospital cafeteria. When his responsibilities forced him to attend a department meeting, he sat near the door, rehearsed his contributions three times before speaking, and left as soon as it ended. The avoidance made the memories more frequent, because he had so few new experiences to crowd them out, and it deepened his isolation—he had lost not only his homeland but any sense of belonging in his adopted city. He was certain that if he tried to explain his history to colleagues, they would not understand, or worse, they would see him as damaged. So he said nothing. The rehearsed conversations became a habit that leaked into his private thoughts: he would catch himself mentally preparing a justification for why he had sat through a full sixty-minute session without once mentioning the torture, even to himself.

What finally brought Ricardo to seek help was a news report about a police raid in his home country, broadcast on a Spanish-language station he had not meant to turn on. The anchor’s voice—rapid, authoritative, with the same cadence as the officers who had interrogated him—triggered a full sensory flashback that left him shaking on his living room floor. That night, he could not distract himself. He called a psychotherapy clinic the next morning. He was most afraid that therapy would force him to remember the blank hours, the moments he had sealed away. But he was also, barely, hoping that someone could teach him to live without the rehearsals, without the constant readiness to explain himself.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause or trigger memories; instead, memories trigger appraisals.
The vignette does not show that negative appraisals create new triggers; triggers lead to appraisals.
The vignette shows triggers evoking memories, not memories causing triggers.
The vignette does not indicate that avoidance or rehearsals generate new triggers.
